name: Omar Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal factory shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and a junior operator on the foam-cutting machine at a mattress factory. I left after secondary school and am still learning blade settings; the lead checks my first cut because a wasted foam block is costly. I like seeing a mattress stacked ready for a family, but a crooked blade takes half a shift to put right. My pay is low, we have less than one month of expenses saved, and only a few similar factories are nearby. My wife and I have two school-age children and a mortgage. I never use AI tools; I keep the cut lengths on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my coworkers a computer may tidy orders, but foam still has to be cut square. I trust the first measured slab more than a neat office printout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even without a big AI change, a cancelled Saturday shift would squeeze the mortgage. We are paid near the bottom, have less than a month saved and cannot easily find another nearby foam line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep cutting foam and ask the lead to check my first slab. I would take any offered paid Saturday shift and put a new amount from it against the mortgage after food and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about ordinary lost hours. A quiet AI story still leaves our family one short pay packet from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the lead check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lead measures the first slab at both ends and looks for a blade track that curves. If it is wrong, we stop before cutting another mattress block.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would an extra Saturday help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would cover a few bills, not make us comfortable. Only if the shift is actually paid would I put extra money against the mortgage.

I would **keep** working paid shifts rather than chase a new screen.
think: A **cancelled** Saturday could squeeze our mortgage.
**Low** pay, little cash and few nearby factories leave little space.
do: **Keep** cutting foam with lead checking first slab.
**Pay** extra mortgage principal from any actually paid Saturday shift.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary hours and the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can order fabric and plan runs, but the cutter still needs a careful hand. I would ask the owner to keep real apprentice shifts if the office schedule gets faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Management might cut junior setup hours or leave fewer paid shifts for people still learning. I am one of those people, and our mortgage will feel a smaller week quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the cutter work and show the lead my paper record of setup time. If paid hours fall for several rotas, I would apply only to a posted nearby foam or packing job whose wage covers mortgage, food and travel; meanwhile we would stop paid weekend outings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours, not only about other workers. I have a family to carry and few places nearby to earn the same wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask about apprentice shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older cutters taught me how a blade pulls before it bends. A written setting is useful, but a new worker needs a paid shift beside someone who knows the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI schedule yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read a printed rota and ask the lead to explain it. I have never used an AI tool and would not call that reading a new skill.

say: **Faster** planning must not remove paid apprentice shifts on the foam line.
A **careful** worker still checks the cut after a blade change.
think: A **smaller** wage would reach our mortgage before our thin savings could help.
do: **Keep** recording paid foam-cutter setup time on paper.
**Apply** after repeated cuts to posted nearby bill-covering factory role.
**Stop** paid outings if the shorter rota persists.

fieldNote: He **distinguishes** office scheduling AI from the hands-on cutter work, and never uses AI himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the family that thinking AI reaches ordering in 2028 when I am forty-five, and capable hands-on robots reach foam cutting around 2031 when I am forty-eight. A robot that measures and feeds blocks could take the junior cutter shifts first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to lose most of my paid hours when that robot works. With two children, a mortgage and less than a month saved, I wake in the night thinking about the next payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working while shifts are paid, but if cuts are announced I would ask my brother whether his delivery business has actual paid hours. I would stop paid outings and ask the lender about a temporary payment plan before arrears; if a posted nearby factory job pays mortgage and bills, I would apply. None of these calls replaces a full cutter wage by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by an expected big wage loss and no reliable way to bridge it. I can list calls, but I cannot make a vacant job appear before the mortgage is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether he has paid delivery shifts on real dates, not just a promise to help. My family would be grateful, but I cannot run a mortgage on goodwill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask about a temporary lower payment before missing one and give the actual new rota. I cannot promise an amount until I know the paid hours.

I would **keep** paid shifts and ask family about real work.
think: I **expect** most cutter hours to go and wake over the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches ordering in 2031 when I am forty-eight, with capable foam-cutting robots around 2034 when I am fifty-one. Five more years means I can keep earning and put something against the mortgage first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect junior cutter hours to shrink eventually. I do not see myself taking an unpaid computer course, but I can get better at the blade and ask which nearby manual jobs really pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working paid cutter shifts and put extra money from any actually paid Saturday against the mortgage after essentials. If the factory later cuts hours, I would apply to a posted nearby packing or cutter role that covers our bills; I would also ask my brother about real paid delivery days if no factory opening appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the later wage gap, but I can use several paid years before it. I do not have to pretend I love a screen to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you improve at the cutter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lead to watch one blade change each week and measure the first two slabs with me. That is practice on a machine I already work, not a new course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no extra Saturday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then there is no extra mortgage payment. I would not call the money in our thin account a new saving.

think: **Junior** hours remain vulnerable, but five years help.
An **unpaid** computer course would take money from the family.

**Pay** extra mortgage principal from any paid Saturday after essentials.

fieldNote: **Omar** improves familiar cutter practice, not a new AI tool or trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children thinking AI reaches orders in 2036 when I am fifty-three, and capable foam-cutting robots around 2039 when I am fifty-six. Ten years is time to work and pay the house down; it is not an early retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will be older, but I will still need wages at fifty-six. I cannot assume the mortgage is gone or a new factory will hire me if the cutter work disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the foam-cutter job, take actually paid Saturday shifts when offered and put extra money toward the mortgage after essentials. I would ask the lead for more safe blade-setting practice, and if later hours fall I would apply only to a posted nearby factory or delivery role that covers the household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a wage loss years away, though the warning gives me more paid time. I will count actual shifts, not imaginary savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would encourage a practical apprenticeship after school if either child wants one, and ask what local employers actually pay apprentices. I would not decide their future from a robot headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a new AI cutter control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI, and I would first ask for an in-person demonstration on a stopped machine. I am not enrolling in a screen course on a guess.

say: **Ten** years means more paid work, not retirement at fifty-six.
think: The **mortgage** and wages still matter after the children grow.
A **future** job must be posted nearby and pay our bills.
do: **Keep** paid cutter shifts and practise blade changes safely.
**Pay** extra mortgage principal from actual Saturday wages.
**Apply** after cuts to posted nearby adequate factory or delivery role.
feel: **Anxious** about later hours, with paid years to prepare.
S4.quote: I will count actual shifts, not imaginary savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable foam-cutting robots around 2031 could take most junior shifts before I can protect the mortgage. Real paid work nearby and time to arrange the house payment would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a father can tell his children the factory still needs him when the paid roster is shrinking. I will ask for work before I ask for charity. A mortgage cannot be paid with a promise of work.

headlineQuote: A mortgage cannot be paid with a promise of work.
portrait: **Omar**, forty-three, is a junior mattress-foam cutter with secondary schooling, a partner and two school-age children.
His **low** pay, mortgage, less than one month saved and few nearby factories create baseline anxiety.
He **never** uses AI and prefers measured blade settings, paid work and family help before a screen course.
**Fast** robots leave him without a reliable wage bridge; longer warning lets him reduce mortgage debt from actual Saturday pay.
biggestWorry: **Capable** foam robots around 2031 could remove most junior paid hours before Omar can protect the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Actual** nearby bill-covering work and a temporary mortgage payment arrangement would help the family bridge lost shifts.
